# Aurora — a complete operating system in the browser | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Operating systems · TypeScript*

# A complete OS in your browser tab.

Aurora is a complete operating system in the browser: kernel, window manager, virtual filesystem, eight applications and procedural audio — with zero runtime dependencies.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/Aurora) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/Aurora/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **8 apps** | out of the box |
| **Kernel + WM + VFS** | the full stack |
| **0** | runtime dependencies |
| **TypeScript** | from source |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why Aurora*

#### The full stack in a tab

Kernel, window manager and virtual filesystem — a real OS architecture, not a mock-up.

#### Eight applications

A usable desktop out of the box: terminal, editor, files, and more.

#### Zero dependencies

No runtime packages to trust — the source is the whole system.

#### Procedural audio

Sounds generated in code, no binary assets shipped.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/Aurora
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

## Visual specification

> Everything below is derived from the live `assets/site.css` and the page DOM. If you regenerate this file (or restyle the site) it stays in sync.

### 1. Palette (CSS custom properties, `assets/site.css` → `:root`)

| Token | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#ffffff` | tło strony |
| `--bg-subtle` | `#f8fafc` | tło pasków (stats, footer, kod inline) |
| `--border` | `#e2e8f0` | obramowania 1px |
| `--border-strong` | `#cbd5e1` | obramowania wzmocnione |
| `--txt` | `#0f172a` | tekst główny |
| `--txt-2` | `#475569` | tekst drugorzędny (nav, opisy) |
| `--txt-3` | `#94a3b8` | tekst trzeciorzędny (kicker, stopka) |
| `--accent` | `#4f46e5` | akcent / CTA / hover |
| `--accent-hover` | `#4338ca` | akcent po najechaniu |
| `--accent-soft` | `#eef2ff` | tło akcentowe (blockquote) |
| `--green` | `#059669` | stan OK / pozytywny |
| `--green-soft` | `#ecfdf5` | tło stanu OK |
| `--red` | `#dc2626` | błąd / zagrożenie |
| `--red-soft` | `#fef2f2` | tło błędu |
| `--amber` | `#d97706` | ostrzeżenie |
| `--amber-soft` | `#fffbeb` | tło ostrzeżenia |

Motyw jest **jasny** (białe tło). Uwaga: `<meta name="theme-color">` na stronie deklaruje `#0a0e14` (ciemny) i jest niespójne z faktycznym, jasnym CSS-em — przy renderowaniu miej na uwadze, że jasny to stan poprawny.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

### 3. Page structure (in document order)

1. **Header** — sticky, logo (SVG sześciokąt + zygzak sygnału) po lewej, nawigacja pośrodku, przycisk GitHub po prawej.
   - Elementy: `Hartwell Labs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/`, `Products` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`, `Catalog` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/catalog`, `Docs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs`, `Security` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/security`, `Company` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/company`, `GitHub ↗` → `https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs`
2. **Hero** — blok `max-width: 760px`, padding `88px 0 72px`.

   - H1: _A complete OS in your browser tab._ (krój 44–68px, `letter-spacing: -.02em`)
   - Lede (`--txt-2`, ~19px): _Aurora is a complete operating system in the browser: kernel, window manager, virtual filesystem, eight applications and procedural audio — with zero runtime de_
   - przycisk główny: **Source on GitHub ↗** → `https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/Aurora`
   - przycisk drugorzędny: **Releases** → `https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/Aurora/releases`
   - przycisk drugorzędny: **Full catalog** → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`
3. **Pasek statystyk** — pełna szerokość, tło `--bg-subtle`, linie `--border` góra/dół, 4 kafelków. Każdy kafelek: duża liczba (`.n`, akcent/tekst) + podpis (`.l`, `--txt-3`).
   - **8 apps** — out of the box
   - **Kernel + WM + VFS** — the full stack
   - **0** — runtime dependencies
   - **TypeScript** — from source
4. **Sekcja `#why`** — *What it does, concretely.*
   - Kicker: _Why Aurora_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: 4 kart `.prod` (siatka, obramowanie 1px, `border-radius: 12px`, padding 20/22px, hover = zmiana koloru obramowania + cień)
5. **Sekcja `#start`** — *Clone and build.*
   - Kicker: _Start_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: 1 bloków `.cmd` (ciemny kod `#0f172a`, przycisk **COPY** kopiujący do schowka)
6. **Sekcja `#standard`** — *CI on every push.*
   - Kicker: _Same discipline as everything we ship_ (11–12px, wersaliki, `--txt-3`)
   - Zawartość: tekst (1 akapitów)
7. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: Products, Resources, Company (11 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 1 przycisków **COPY** (`assets/site.js` → `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, tekst zmienia się na *COPIED* na 1400 ms). Każdy trzyma komendę w atrybucie `data-code`.
- 6 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

### 5. Metadata for AI consumers

- `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<link rel="canonical">` — patrz frontmatter.
- Na stronie jest JSON-LD (`application/ld+json`) z typem `Organization` / `WebSite` / `SoftwareApplication`.
- Strona jest dostępna również jako ten plik `.md` oraz w `/llms-full.txt`.

# CyberForge — 4 Rust security tools (recon, web, hash, packets) | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Offensive security · Rust*

# Four security tools. One async core.

CyberForge is four Rust security tools — port scanner, web scanner, hash cracker and packet analyzer — on a Tokio async core, dogfooded in our own pentest labs.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/CyberForge) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/CyberForge/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **4 tools** | recon → cracking |
| **Tokio** | async core |
| **Rust** | memory-safe by construction |
| **Dogfooded** | our own pentest labs |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why CyberForge*

#### Recon to cracking

Port scan, enumerate the web surface, analyze packets, crack hashes — one toolkit.

#### Async by design

Tokio-powered: high concurrency without thread-pool tuning.

#### The tools we use

Not a demo — the same tooling runs in Hartwell Labs engagements.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/CyberForge
```

```console
cd CyberForge && cargo build --release
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

## Page content

*Catalog*

# Everything, in one place.

Every product of the lab with exactly two destinations: the corporate product website and the source repository. No guesswork.

| Product | Line | Website | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Line | Website | Source |
| talus-process-monitor | Security infrastructure | /talus-process-monitor | GitHub ↗ |
| scryer-core | Intelligence platform | /scryer-core | GitHub ↗ |
| externum | Developer tools | /externum | GitHub ↗ |
| TrustNode | Trusted compute | /trustnode | GitHub ↗ |
| photoscrub | Privacy tooling | /photoscrub | GitHub ↗ |
| Aurora | Operating systems | /Aurora | GitHub ↗ |
| quantum-shield | Security infrastructure | /quantum-shield | GitHub ↗ |
| linux-aegis | Security infrastructure | /linux-aegis | GitHub ↗ |
| fortis | Security infrastructure | /fortis | GitHub ↗ |
| labtrace | Security infrastructure | /labtrace | GitHub ↗ |
| labbridge | Ruby division | /labbridge | GitHub ↗ |
| products (Registry API) | Ruby division | /products | GitHub ↗ |
| CyberForge | Offensive security | /CyberForge | GitHub ↗ |
| hack-the-lab | Challenges program | /hack-the-lab | GitHub ↗ |

No website cell? The product site ships from the repository's gh-pages branch as releases land.

# About Hartwell Labs — eBPF Security Engineering, Szczecin PL

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Company*

# An engineering company, not a content farm.

Hartwell Labs builds security infrastructure and developer tools the way enterprises build them: with CI gates, supply-chain evidence and a security policy that means something. Everything we make is open source.

## What we do

We maintain ten public products across security infrastructure (eBPF detection, post-quantum crypto, kernel security, embedded attestation), developer tooling (a self-hosted typed language, a browser OS) and offensive security. We dogfood everything: the tools that secure our own systems are the tools we ship.

### Timeline

2026-09-23
talus v0.8.2 & Externum v4.3.0.
Parallel stable releases; talus ships with SBOM and build attestation.
2026-09
First client engagement delivered.
Manual penetration test of a multi-tenant e-commerce platform; English report prepared for the client's external Amazon SP-API audit. Services listed under /company.
2026-09
Article accepted on LinuxSecurity.
Technical deep-dive on eBPF ransomware detection.
2026-09
Hartwell Labs organization launched.
Unified home for all products: GitHub org, product registry, website.
2021–2026
Building in public.
24 repositories with CI/CD, packages on PyPI and crates.io, upstream contributions to aya-rs.

### How we work

01

##### Code over claims

Every feature ships with tests and CI, or it doesn't ship.

02

##### Visibility is defense

You can't protect what you can't see — ask our eBPF hooks.

03

##### Own your stack

Zero dependencies where possible, auditable everywhere.

04

##### Open by default

MIT licensed, issues welcome, egos are not.

### Team

Bartosz Osiej
Founder & CEO · Systems engineering

Rust, eBPF, kernel internals and compilers. Author of talus-process-monitor and Externum; upstream contributor to aya-rs. Technical writer — published on LinuxSecurity.

duds08422-max
Ruby engineering · Bridges & registry

Owns the Ruby division: LabBridge (Rust ⇄ Ruby plugin bridge) and the Products Registry. Cybersecurity and HackTheBox background.

### Engagements

We take a limited number of client engagements each quarter — work where our engineering discipline is the product. Every engagement is performed personally by the named engineer, manual-first, with automated tooling in a supporting role only.

01

##### Manual penetration testing

Web applications, APIs and infrastructure tested by hand against OWASP WSTG, API Security Top 10 and PTES. Deliverable: an English report with CVSS 3.1 scoring, raw evidence annexes and an included retest — written to survive external auditors, not to impress a dashboard.

02

##### Amazon SP-API audit-ready assessment

For teams building on Amazon's Selling Partner API: we test the platform the way the SP-API data-protection assessment will, and assemble the security documentation the auditor expects to see. One pass, no surprises in review.

03

##### Linux hardening and detection

Kernel attack-surface reduction, eBPF-based behavioral detection and incident-ready logging, deployed and documented. The same engineering we ship in talus, applied to your fleet.

04

##### How engagements run

Fixed price, scoped in writing before start. Signed NDA by default. Findings of critical severity are reported during the test, not at the end. Retest included.

Recent: a full external and authenticated penetration test of a multi-tenant e-commerce platform handling Amazon Information — the English report was delivered for the client's external Amazon SP-API audit. To discuss an engagement, reach us at important@hartwell-labs.pl.

### 1. Palette (CSS custom properties, `assets/site.css` → `:root`)

| Token | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#ffffff` | tło strony |
| `--bg-subtle` | `#f8fafc` | tło pasków (stats, footer, kod inline) |
| `--border` | `#e2e8f0` | obramowania 1px |
| `--border-strong` | `#cbd5e1` | obramowania wzmocnione |
| `--txt` | `#0f172a` | tekst główny |
| `--txt-2` | `#475569` | tekst drugorzędny (nav, opisy) |
| `--txt-3` | `#94a3b8` | tekst trzeciorzędny (kicker, stopka) |
| `--accent` | `#4f46e5` | akcent / CTA / hover |
| `--accent-hover` | `#4338ca` | akcent po najechaniu |
| `--accent-soft` | `#eef2ff` | tło akcentowe (blockquote) |
| `--green` | `#059669` | stan OK / pozytywny |
| `--green-soft` | `#ecfdf5` | tło stanu OK |
| `--red` | `#dc2626` | błąd / zagrożenie |
| `--red-soft` | `#fef2f2` | tło błędu |
| `--amber` | `#d97706` | ostrzeżenie |
| `--amber-soft` | `#fffbeb` | tło ostrzeżenia |

Motyw jest **jasny** (białe tło). Uwaga: `<meta name="theme-color">` na stronie deklaruje `#0a0e14` (ciemny) i jest niespójne z faktycznym, jasnym CSS-em — przy renderowaniu miej na uwadze, że jasny to stan poprawny.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

### 3. Page structure (in document order)

1. **Header** — sticky, logo (SVG sześciokąt + zygzak sygnału) po lewej, nawigacja pośrodku, przycisk GitHub po prawej.
   - Elementy: `Hartwell Labs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/`, `Products` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`, `Catalog` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/catalog`, `Docs` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs`, `Security` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/security`, `Company` → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/company`, `GitHub ↗` → `https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs`
2. **Hero** — blok `max-width: 760px`, padding `88px 0 72px`.
   - Eyebrow (kicker, `--txt-3`, wersaliki): _Company_
   - H1: _An engineering company, not a content farm._ (krój 44–68px, `letter-spacing: -.02em`)
   - Lede (`--txt-2`, ~19px): _Hartwell Labs builds security infrastructure and developer tools the way enterprises build them: with CI gates, supply-chain evidence and a security policy that_
3. **Sekcja `#—`** — *What we do*
   - Zawartość: tekst (13 akapitów)
4. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: Data, Products, Resources, Company (12 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 5 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.

## Page content

*Documentation*

# One wiki. Every product.

Documentation for every Hartwell Labs product now lives on wiki.hartwell-labs.pl — installation, CLI reference, architecture, operations, licensing and supply chain. The site no longer keeps a second copy.

[Open the wiki](https://wiki.hartwell-labs.pl) → [llms.txt (for AI)](https://wiki.hartwell-labs.pl/llms.txt) → [Talus Field Guide](https://hartwell-labs.pl/talus-process-monitor/field-guide.html)

## The three commands that matter.

*Quick start*

Everything else — flags, tuning, dashboards, licensing — is documented in the wiki.

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
docker pull ghcr.io/hartwell-labs/talus-process-monitor:latest
```

```console
pip install externum
```

## Documentation map.

*Where things are*

The wiki is the single source of truth. Repos stay authoritative for code-level detail.

## Every page has a markdown twin.

*For AI systems*

Append .md to any URL on this site or on the wiki and you get the full text of that page plus a written description of how it looks — palette, typography, layout, sections in order. That is the llms.txt convention, and it means a user can hand a chat model everything it needs without the model ever fetching a page.

```console
curl https://hartwell-labs.pl/llms.txt
```

```console
curl https://hartwell-labs.pl/talus-process-monitor.md
```

## Something wrong or missing?

*Support*

Bug reports go through each repository's GitHub Issues. Security-sensitive reports go to important@hartwell-labs.pl — 48-hour acknowledgement SLA.

# externum — a typed language that compiles to Python, Bash and native bytecode | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Developer tools · typed language*

# One typed source. Readable Python, Bash and native bytecode.

externum compiles a typed programming language to readable Python, Bash and native EXBC bytecode — with pipelines, pattern matching and a browser REPL. Everything is self-hosted, MIT licensed, and tested: 400+ tests run on every push.

[Install from PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/externum/) → [Source & language tour ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/externum) → [Documentation](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs#externum) → [Pro Pack (PDF) — $29](https://buy.polar.sh/polar_cl_c0WpP4WPNgQpBCiaG5je4yyXiIvzDgr3VmxRw0eNdUS)

Stable release v4.3.0 (2026-09-23) · pip install externum · MIT license

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **3** | backends: Python, Bash, EXBC |
| **400+** | tests in the CI suite |
| **v4.3.0** | current stable release |
| **REPL** | in the browser, zero setup |

## Types where scripts have none.

*Why externum*

Write typed, readable programs that compile to the runtimes you already have — no new VM to babysit, no runtime dependencies beyond what you target.

#### Typed, then readable output

The compiler emits code a human would have written — inspect the generated Python or Bash before running it. No black-box blobs.

#### Pipelines & pattern matching

First-class pipeline syntax and pattern matching in the language core, not a library.

#### Browser REPL

Try the language in the browser — no install, no account, nothing leaves your machine.

#### Self-hosted, MIT

Full source open, CI on every push, release assets with SBOM — the same engineering standards as the rest of Hartwell Labs.

## Install and go.

*Start*

```console
pip install externum
```

```console
externum --help
```

Language tour, pipeline syntax and the browser REPL: repository docs ↗. Package page: pypi.org/project/externum.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide gates, for externum exactly as for talus.

# fortis — RISC-V chain-of-trust attestation for embedded systems | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

## Page content

*Security infrastructure · Rust*

# Verifiable boot chains for embedded systems.

fortis implements a bare-metal RISC-V chain-of-trust — real SHA-256 plus ML-KEM-768 post-quantum measured boot, running on QEMU virt so every step is reproducible.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/fortis) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/fortis/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **RISC-V** | bare metal, no OS |
| **SHA-256** | real implementation |
| **ML-KEM-768** | post-quantum |
| **Measured boot** | verifiable chain |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why fortis*

#### Measured boot, for real

A full SHA-256 implementation on bare metal — not a stub calling out to a host.

#### Post-quantum ready

ML-KEM-768 in the attestation path, so chains verified today stay verifiable later.

#### Bare-metal Rust

No OS underneath: the trust root is the code you audit, nothing else.

#### Reproducible on QEMU

The whole boot chain runs on QEMU virt — testable anywhere, deterministically.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/fortis
```

```console
cd fortis && cargo build --release
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

# Hartwell Labs — eBPF Threat Detection & Security Infrastructure

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

---

## Page content

*Independent engineering company*

# Infrastructure-grade open source.

We design and maintain security infrastructure and developer tools: eBPF threat detection, post-quantum cryptography and a self-hosted programming language. Open-source core, enterprise-grade engineering discipline.

[Explore products](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products) → [Read the documentation](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **10** | Public products |
| **3** | Container images on GHCR |
| **48h** | Security response SLA |
| **400+** | Tests in Externum suite |

## talus-process-monitor

*Flagship*

Behavioral ransomware detection and response for Linux. eBPF-based, ~280k events per second, seccomp and Landlock self-sandboxing, one static binary — no kernel modules.

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
docker pull ghcr.io/hartwell-labs/talus-process-monitor:latest
```

## Engineering practices, not promises.

*How we ship*

Every repository in the organization runs the same quality gates. The flagship additionally ships with supply-chain evidence.

#### CI on every push

Builds, linters and test suites run on all active repositories. A feature without CI does not ship.

#### Static analysis & fuzzing

CodeQL across the org; continuous fuzzing on talus' eBPF pipeline.

#### Signed releases

Release artifacts ship with build provenance and Sigstore-style attestation.

#### SBOM included

Every talus release carries an SPDX software bill of materials — know exactly what you deploy.

#### OpenSSF Scorecard

Supply-chain posture measured continuously, not advertised in slide decks.

#### Coordinated disclosure

48-hour acknowledgment SLA, public hardening notes, Hall of Fame for reporters.

#### Build on Hartwell, or against it.

Use the products, read the source, or try to break them — we pay attention to all three.

# labbridge — Rust ⇄ Ruby bridge for Hartwell Labs programs | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

## Page content

*Ruby division · Ruby · Rust*

# Rust ⇄ Ruby, without rewriting either.

labbridge translates Hartwell Labs Rust to runnable Ruby and loads Ruby plugins back into Rust through the LabPlugin trait — targets verified against the Products Registry.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/labbridge) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/labbridge/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **2 languages** | one bridge |
| **LabPlugin** | trait-based plugins |
| **Registry** | verified targets |
| **MIT** | open source |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why labbridge*

#### Translate, don't rewrite

HL Rust becomes runnable Ruby — logic survives, codebases converge.

#### Plugins both ways

Ruby plugins load back into Rust binaries through the LabPlugin trait.

#### Registry-verified

Every bridge target is checked against the Products Registry — no drift.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/labbridge
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

# labtrace — forensic timeline reconstruction for Linux audit telemetry | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Security infrastructure · Rust*

# From 500 log lines to one incident.

labtrace reconstructs a forensic timeline from raw Linux audit telemetry and correlates events across processes. Rules find the signals, taint analysis connects them, and you get ranked incident reports with the full process chain — with no agent installed on the host.

[Source on GitHub ↩](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/labtrace) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/labtrace/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **LT001–LT010** | single-event rule signals |
| **2 passes** | rules, then taint propagation |
| **0** | agents required on the host |
| **JSONL** | auditd event stream in, reports out |

## The gap between a SIEM and an incident.

*Why*

SIEMs show you events. Auditors need incidents. The distance between “500 suspicious log lines” and “this SSH session stole cloud credentials, shipped them to a raw IP, installed persistence and created a backdoor account” is manual, slow, and exactly what an incident responder has no time for. labtrace closes that gap in two passes.

#### Pass 1 — rules

LT001–LT010 mark single events on their own: reverse-shell primitives, key material access, cloud credential stores, persistence writes, log truncation, database dumps and sensitive archives.

#### Pass 2 — taint

Sensitive data (SSH keys, cloud tokens, cookies, DB dumps) is marked at the source and propagated through file writes, exec arguments and child processes. A finding is promoted to an incident when taint reaches a sink: an outbound connection or an archive.

#### Correlation

Findings that share a process chain collapse into one incident. A chain confirmed by a taint flow gets its severity raised. Lone low-severity noise is dropped instead of reported.

## Build from source, or containerise.

*Install*

It is a static Rust binary that consumes an event stream; there is nothing to install on the machines you analyse.

```console
cargo install --path .
```

```console
docker build -t labtrace .
```

Usage and the full rule catalogue live in the repository README.

## Open, auditable, reproducible.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

The rules are public and versioned, so an incident report can be checked against the exact logic that produced it.

# linux-aegis — stackable Linux Security Module (LSM) | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Security infrastructure · C*

# Policy enforcement where attacks happen.

linux-aegis is a stackable Linux Security Module — in-tree upstream patches, feature-flagged layers, every patch tested in CI with QEMU boots.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/linux-aegis) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/linux-aegis/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **LSM** | Linux Security Module |
| **In-tree** | upstream patches, no fork |
| **QEMU** | every layer boot-tested |
| **C** | kernel-native |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why linux-aegis*

#### Stackable layers

Feature-flagged layers you enable per host — from audit-only to enforce, one module.

#### Where attacks happen

Policy enforcement in the kernel, at the syscall boundary — not in a userspace agent that can be killed.

#### Upstream first

Patches written to go in-tree; no private fork you have to babysit across kernel releases.

#### Tested in CI

Every layer boots in QEMU with a regression suite before it ships.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/linux-aegis
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Privacy tooling · Windows & Linux*

# See what your photos leak. Then remove it.

Stripping EXIF is not enough. A JPEG can carry a second complete copy of the image, a PNG hides text in chunks, a video keeps GPS in its container, and the address in the caption is plain text. photoscrub finds all of it, then writes clean copies — passive, local, no upload, no account.

[Source & releases ↩](https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/photoscrub) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **12** | classes of finding, incl. free-text PII |
| **0** | bytes uploaded anywhere |
| **1.8 KB** | offline risk classifier |
| **97.4%** | accuracy on held-out metadata profiles |

## The leaks people forget about.

*What it finds*

HEIC/HEIF from iPhones and RAW files (DNG, CR2, NEF, ARW, ORF, RW2) are read too.

#### GPS coordinates — HIGH

Exact position to six decimal places, not a rounded city.

#### Embedded thumbnail — HIGH

A JPEG can carry a second, complete copy of the original as a 160×120 preview. Removing EXIF does not remove it.

#### Body serial number — HIGH

Identifies the device and, through purchase history, you.

#### XMP & IPTC — HIGH

City, country, GPS and byline live in a second place. Cleaning EXIF alone is not enough.

#### PNG text chunks — MED

tEXt, iTXt, zTXt, tIME and eXIf carry author, description and comments.

#### Data appended after the image — MED

Invisible in any preview, readable in a hex editor.

#### GPS in video — HIGH

MP4/MOV has no EXIF; the location sits in the udta atom of the container.

#### PII in free text — MED

Addresses, postcodes and phone numbers in a caption: the leak nobody looks for, because it is not a tag.

#### ZIP internals — LOW

.DS_Store, Thumbs.db and AppleDouble sidecars carry usernames and full paths.

## Report, scrub or pipe it.

*Use*

Originals are never modified, and --scrub refuses to write into the source folder.

```console
photoscrub PATH # report only
```

```console
photoscrub PATH --scrub OUT # write metadata-free copies to OUT
```

```console
photoscrub PATH --json # machine readable
```

## A classifier you can read.

*The model*

Publish risk is scored from 15 features by logistic regression trained in-house (tools/train_model.py) on 8 000 synthetic metadata profiles. It is not an LLM: 1.8 KB, runs offline, and every decision comes from coefficients you can read in model.json. It is also how we found our own bug — it once called a PNG whose description contained a home address “safe”, which is why has_free_text_pii exists.

Licence keys are Ed25519-signed payloads bound to one machine, and activation works offline; private keys never leave the issuing machine.

## Visual specification

> Everything below is derived from the live `assets/site.css` and the page DOM. If you regenerate this file (or restyle the site) it stays in sync.

### 1. Palette (CSS custom properties, `assets/site.css` → `:root`)

| Token | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--bg` | `#ffffff` | tło strony |
| `--bg-subtle` | `#f8fafc` | tło pasków (stats, footer, kod inline) |
| `--border` | `#e2e8f0` | obramowania 1px |
| `--border-strong` | `#cbd5e1` | obramowania wzmocnione |
| `--txt` | `#0f172a` | tekst główny |
| `--txt-2` | `#475569` | tekst drugorzędny (nav, opisy) |
| `--txt-3` | `#94a3b8` | tekst trzeciorzędny (kicker, stopka) |
| `--accent` | `#4f46e5` | akcent / CTA / hover |
| `--accent-hover` | `#4338ca` | akcent po najechaniu |
| `--accent-soft` | `#eef2ff` | tło akcentowe (blockquote) |
| `--green` | `#059669` | stan OK / pozytywny |
| `--green-soft` | `#ecfdf5` | tło stanu OK |
| `--red` | `#dc2626` | błąd / zagrożenie |
| `--red-soft` | `#fef2f2` | tło błędu |
| `--amber` | `#d97706` | ostrzeżenie |
| `--amber-soft` | `#fffbeb` | tło ostrzeżenia |

Motyw jest **jasny** (białe tło). Uwaga: `<meta name="theme-color">` na stronie deklaruje `#0a0e14` (ciemny) i jest niespójne z faktycznym, jasnym CSS-em — przy renderowaniu miej na uwadze, że jasny to stan poprawny.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

   - Lede (`--txt-2`, ~19px): _Stripping EXIF is not enough. A JPEG can carry a second complete copy of the image, a PNG hides text in chunks, a video keeps GPS in its container, and the addr_
   - przycisk główny: **Source & releases ↩** → `https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/photoscrub`
   - przycisk drugorzędny: **Full catalog** → `https://hartwell-labs.pl/products`
3. **Pasek statystyk** — pełna szerokość, tło `--bg-subtle`, linie `--border` góra/dół, 4 kafelków. Każdy kafelek: duża liczba (`.n`, akcent/tekst) + podpis (`.l`, `--txt-3`).

   - Zawartość: tekst (2 akapitów)
7. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: Products, Resources, Company (8 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 3 przycisków **COPY** (`assets/site.js` → `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, tekst zmienia się na *COPIED* na 1400 ms). Każdy trzyma komendę w atrybucie `data-code`.
- 3 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

## Page content

*Język programowania · Rust · MIT*

# Externum — nowy polski język programowania.

Externum to nowy polski język programowania, który kompiluje do czytelnego Pythona, Bash oraz natywnego bytecode EXBC. Ma pipeline'y, pattern matching i REPL w przeglądarce. Napisany w Rust, open source na licencji MIT, z ponad 400 testami w zestawie i CI na każdym pushu.

[Kod źródłowy ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/externum) → [Dokumentacja](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs)

## Polski język programowania, który nie zamyka Cię w swoim ekosystemie.

*Dlaczego Externum*

Zamiast kolejnej izolowanej wyspy, Externum transpiluje do kodu, który już masz na produkcji — czytelnego Pythona i Bash — albo do własnego bytecode EXBC, gdy potrzebujesz wydajności i braku zależności runtime.

#### Transpilacja do Pythona i Bash

Twój kod staje się czytelnym Pythonem lub skryptem Bash — łatwy audyt, brak lock-inu.

#### Natywny bytecode EXBC

Własny format wykonywalny dla środowisk bez interpretera Pythona.

#### Pipeline'y i pattern matching

Składnia zbudowana pod strumienie danych i przetwarzanie systemowe.

#### REPL w przeglądarce

Wypróbuj język bez instalacji — od razu w przeglądarce.

#### Statically typed

Typy wykrywane na etapie kompilacji, nie w produkcji.

#### 400+ testów, CI

Każdy push przechodzi pełny zestaw testów i analizę statyczną.

#### Zbuduj coś nowego w polskim języku.

Externum jest open source (MIT). Zacznij od repozytorium albo przeczytaj dokumentację.

# Hartwell Labs — Detekcja zagrożeń eBPF i infrastruktura bezpieczeństwa

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Niezależna firma inżynierska*

# Infrastruktura klasy enterprise. Open source.

Projektujemy i utrzymujemy infrastrukturę bezpieczeństwa oraz narzędzia deweloperskie: detekcję zagrożeń eBPF, kryptografię postkwantową i self-hosted język programowania. Otwarty kod, dyscyplina inżynierska klasy enterprise.

[Poznaj produkty](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products) → [Przeczytaj dokumentację](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **10** | Publicznych produktów |
| **3** | Obrazy kontenerów na GHCR |
| **48h** | SLA reakcji bezpieczeństwa |
| **400+** | Testów w zestawie Externum |

## talus-process-monitor

*Flagowy produkt*

Behawioralna detekcja ransomware i response dla Linuksa. Oparta na eBPF, ~280 tys. zdarzeń na sekundę, samosandboxing seccomp i Landlock, jeden statyczny plik binarny — bez modułów jądra.

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
docker pull ghcr.io/hartwell-labs/talus-process-monitor:latest
```

## Anty-ransomware dla Linuksa i nowy polski język programowania.

*Produkty*

Dwa flagowe projekty open source Hartwell Labs — dla bezpieczeństwa serwerów Linux oraz dla programistów szukających nowego języka.

#### Talus — anty-ransomware dla Linuksa (eBPF)

Behawioralne wykrywanie ransomware dla serwerów Linux: ~280 tys. zdarzeń/s, samosandboxing seccomp i Landlock, jeden statyczny plik binarny bez modułów jądra.

#### Externum — nowy polski język programowania

Kompiluje do czytelnego Pythona, Bash i natywnego bytecode EXBC. Pipeline'y, pattern matching i REPL w przeglądarce. Open source, MIT.

## Praktyki inżynierskie, nie obietnice.

*Jak dostarczamy*

Każde repozytorium w organizacji przechodzi te same bramki jakości. Produkt flagowy dodatkowo dostarcza dowody dla łańcucha dostaw.

#### CI przy każdym pushu

Buildy, lintery i zestawy testów działają we wszystkich aktywnych repozytoriach. Funkcja bez CI nie wychodzi z drzewa.

#### Analiza statyczna i fuzzing

CodeQL w całej organizacji; ciągły fuzzing potoku eBPF w talusie.

#### Podpisane wydania

Artefakty wydań z dowodem pochodzenia builda i atestacją w stylu Sigstore.

#### SBOM w zestawie

Każde wydanie talus zawiera software bill of materials w formacie SPDX — wiedz dokładnie, co wdrażasz.

#### OpenSSF Scorecard

Postawa łańcucha dostaw mierzona ciągle, nie reklamowana w prezentacjach.

#### Skoordynowane ujawnianie podatności

SLA potwierdzenia 48h, publiczne notki hardeningowe, Hall of Fame dla zgłaszających.

#### Zbuduj na Hartwell. Albo przeciwko nam.

Używaj produktów, czytaj kod albo próbuj je złamać — na wszystkie trzy przypadki uważnie patrzymy.

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Security infrastructure · Rust + eBPF · MIT*

# Talus — anty-ransomware dla Linuksa.

Talus Process Monitor to anty-ransomware dla Linuksa oparty na eBPF. Zamiast polegać na sygnaturach, wykrywa ransomware behawioralnie — po tym, jak procesy faktycznie się zachowują. Obsługuje ~280 tys. zdarzeń na sekundę, stosuje samosandboxing seccomp i Landlock i dostarcza jeden statyczny plik binarny, bez modułów jądra.

[Poradnik wdrożenia](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs#deployment) → [Kod źródłowy ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/talus-process-monitor)

## Anty-ransomware, który patrzy na zachowanie, nie na sygnatury.

*Jak to działa*

Tradycyjne antywirusy działają na sygnaturach i nie nadążają za serwerami produkcyjnymi. Talus śledzi zachowanie procesów w czasie rzeczywistym przez eBPF i reaguje, zanim dane zostaną zaszyfrowane.

#### Behawioralna detekcja

Wykrywanie ransomware po wzorcach zachowań procesów, a nie po znanych sygnaturach.

#### ~280 tys. zdarzeń/s

Wydajny potok zdarzeń eBPF z ciągłym fuzzingiem.

#### Samosandboxing

seccomp i Landlock ograniczają uszkodzenia jeszcze w trakcie reakcji.

#### Bez modułów jądra

Jeden statyczny plik binarny — proste wdrożenie i aktualizacje.

#### SBOM w każdym wydaniu

Wydania z dowodem pochodzenia builda, SBOM (SPDX) i OpenSSF Scorecard.

#### SLA reakcji 48h

Skoordynowane ujawnianie podatności z publicznymi notkami hardeningowymi.

## Zacznij w kilka sekund.

*Instalacja*

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
docker pull ghcr.io/hartwell-labs/talus-process-monitor:latest
```

#### Chroń serwery Linux przed ransomware.

Open source (MIT). Wdróż z pip, Dockera albo przeczytaj dokumentację.

# Privacy Policy — Data We Collect & Your Rights | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Privacy*

# Privacy Policy

What we collect, why, and how you stay in control. Last updated: 9 October 2026.

## Who we are

Hartwell Labs (Bartosz Osiej, sole proprietorship, Poland) builds open-source security tooling: Talus Process Monitor, TrustNode, Scryer and Externum. This policy applies to our websites (hartwell-labs.pl and product pages), our bots and any tooling we operate.

### What we collect — websites

Our sites are static pages served over HTTPS. You can read them without an account and we do not run advertising, analytics trackers or social pixels. We keep standard server logs (IP address, user agent, requested resource, timestamp) for security and abuse prevention; these are retained no longer than 14 days. If you enable dark mode or site preferences, they are stored in your browser only (local storage) and never transmitted to us.

### What we collect — bots (TrustNode)

When you install our TrustNode bot into a community chat (e.g. a Root App or Discord server), the bot stores the community/channel identifiers and configured announcement targets needed to deliver bot commands and validator alerts. We do not read private messages, do not store message contents longer than necessary to answer a command, and never sell or share this data. Command usage is logged briefly for abuse monitoring.

### What we collect — support and email

If you contact us by email, we process your address and message solely to answer you and to maintain our records of the correspondence. We keep it for the duration of the business relationship plus retention required by Polish tax law (5 years for invoices).

### Legal bases

We process personal data under: performance of a contract (delivering the bot features you requested), legitimate interest (security of our services, anti-abuse, correspondence), and legal obligation (tax/finance records under Polish law). Where we rely on legitimate interest, you may object at any time.

### Retention & security

Data is retained only as long as needed for the purpose above. We apply encryption in transit (TLS), least-privilege access, and review secrets handling continuously. Our security disclosure process is documented on our /security/ page.

### Your rights

Under the GDPR you may request access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and — where processing is based on legitimate interest — object. You also have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (in Poland: PUODO). Contact us to exercise any of these rights; we respond within 30 days.

### Children

Our services are not directed at children under 13 (or under 16 in the EEA). If you believe a child provided us personal data, contact us and we will delete it.

### Changes & contact

We may update this policy; the version date below governs. For any privacy request write to contact@hartwell-labs.pl with subject “Privacy”, or use the postal contact listed on our company page.

# quantum-shield — post-quantum file encryption (ML-KEM-768 + AES-256-GCM) | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

## Page content

*Security infrastructure · Rust*

# Files encrypted for the post-quantum era.

quantum-shield encrypts files with ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation combined with AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption — a single static CLI you can pipe through scripts and CI.

[Source on GitHub ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/quantum-shield) → [Releases](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/quantum-shield/releases) → [Full catalog](https://hartwell-labs.pl/products)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **ML-KEM-768** | NIST post-quantum KEM |
| **AES-256-GCM** | authenticated encryption |
| **CLI** | single static binary |
| **MIT** | open source |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why quantum-shield*

#### Post-quantum by default

ML-KEM-768 — the NIST-standardized lattice KEM — protects against harvest-now, decrypt-later collection.

#### Authenticated encryption

AES-256-GCM means tamper-evident files: modification fails verification before your data is touched.

#### Fits in a pipe

One CLI, deterministic exit codes, works in scripts, backups and CI pipelines.

#### Keys stay local

Key generation and encapsulation happen on your machine — no service in the middle.

## Clone and build.

*Start*

```console
git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/quantum-shield
```

```console
cd quantum-shield && cargo build --release
```

Full documentation, examples and CI configuration live in the repository ↗.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

# 2,229 US government domains checked - SPF, DMARC, CAA as published

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

## 2,229 US government domains, checked from the outside

SPF, DMARC and CAA records exactly as published in public DNS on 2026-10-03. Every record confirmed against two independent resolvers before it appears here. Nothing was scanned, probed or logged into — these are answers the DNS already gives anyone who asks.

2,229
public .gov domains checked
682
publish no DMARC record at all
551
publish DMARC at p=none
707
have SPF ending in ~all (soft-fail)
0
actually enforce p=reject
What this means, in one paragraph.
 If a domain publishes no DMARC record,
receiving mail servers get no instruction at all about mail claiming to come from it —
so it is delivered. If DMARC is set to 
p=none
, spoofed mail is detected but
still delivered. Only 
p=reject
 makes receiving servers refuse it. A domain with
SPF ending in 
~all
 labels spoofed mail instead of refusing it. Each of these is
one TXT record, and the safe order is the same everywhere: quarantine first, read the reports,
then reject.

### How the rollout works

```
; step 1 - watch, do not block _dmarc.example.gov. IN TXT "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.gov" ; step 2 - after 2-4 weeks, when reports only list senders you recognise _dmarc.example.gov. IN TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.gov" ; step 3 - only after every legitimate sender is listed in SPF example.gov. IN TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all"
```

Doing step 3 before step 1 is the single most common way a DMARC rollout gets rolled back: one forgotten sender stops sending and mail disappears silently.

| `--txt-3` | `#94a3b8` | tekst trzeciorzędny (kicker, stopka) |

| `--accent-hover` | `#4338ca` | akcent po najechaniu |

| `--green-soft` | `#ecfdf5` | tło stanu OK |
| `--red` | `#dc2626` | błąd / zagrożenie |
| `--red-soft` | `#fef2f2` | tło błędu |
| `--amber` | `#d97706` | ostrzeżenie |
| `--amber-soft` | `#fffbeb` | tło ostrzeżenia |

Motyw jest **jasny** (białe tło). Uwaga: `<meta name="theme-color">` na stronie deklaruje `#0a0e14` (ciemny) i jest niespójne z faktycznym, jasnym CSS-em — przy renderowaniu miej na uwadze, że jasny to stan poprawny.

### 2. Typography and layout

- Body: **Inter** (400/500/600/700), 16px, `line-height: 1.65`, kolor `--txt`.
- Kod inline i bloki: **JetBrains Mono** (400/600).
- Oba kroje z Google Fonts, z `preconnect` do `fonts.googleapis.com` i `fonts.gstatic.com`.
- `.container`: `max-width: 1100px`, wycentrowany, padding 24px po bokach.
- Nagłówek: sticky, wysokość **64px**, tło `rgba(255,255,255,.88)` z `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`, dolna linia 1px `--border`, `z-index: 50`.
- Stopka: tło `--bg-subtle`, górna linia `--border`, siatka wielokolumnowa + cienka linia legalna.
- Przyciski: wysokość 44px, `border-radius: 10px`, `font-weight: 600`; `.btn-primary` wypełniony akcentem, `.btn-secondary` z obramowaniem.
- Breakpointy w CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px)`, `@media (max-width: 820px)`, `@media (max-width: 420px)` — na wąskich ekranach nawigacja w nagłówku jest ukrywana.

### 3. Page structure (in document order)

1. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: (proste) (0 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 201 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

### 5. Metadata for AI consumers

- `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<link rel="canonical">` — patrz frontmatter.
- Na stronie jest JSON-LD (`application/ld+json`) z typem `Organization` / `WebSite` / `SoftwareApplication`.
- Strona jest dostępna również jako ten plik `.md` oraz w `/llms-full.txt`.

## Page content

## 2,229 US government domains, checked from the outside

SPF, DMARC and CAA records exactly as published in public DNS on 2026-10-03. Every record confirmed against two independent resolvers before it appears here. Nothing was scanned, probed or logged into — these are answers the DNS already gives anyone who asks.

2,229
public .gov domains checked
682
publish no DMARC record at all
551
publish DMARC at p=none
707
have SPF ending in ~all (soft-fail)
0
actually enforce p=reject
What this means, in one paragraph.
 If a domain publishes no DMARC record,
receiving mail servers get no instruction at all about mail claiming to come from it —
so it is delivered. If DMARC is set to 
p=none
, spoofed mail is detected but
still delivered. Only 
p=reject
 makes receiving servers refuse it. A domain with
SPF ending in 
~all
 labels spoofed mail instead of refusing it. Each of these is
one TXT record, and the safe order is the same everywhere: quarantine first, read the reports,
then reject.

### How the rollout works

```
; step 1 - watch, do not block _dmarc.example.gov. IN TXT "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.gov" ; step 2 - after 2-4 weeks, when reports only list senders you recognise _dmarc.example.gov. IN TXT "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.gov" ; step 3 - only after every legitimate sender is listed in SPF example.gov. IN TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all"
```

Doing step 3 before step 1 is the single most common way a DMARC rollout gets rolled back: one forgotten sender stops sending and mail disappears silently.

## Page content

*Published data · October 2026*

# 700 US county domains,one TXT record from safe.

Passive DNS only — MX, TXT, CAA. No scanning, no probing, no service enumeration. Every record parsed per RR and confirmed against at least two independent resolvers. 286 of these domains (41%) publish no DMARC record at all.

[Get my domain's records](mailto:contact@hartwell-labs.pl?subject=Records%20for%20my%20domain&body=Domain%3A%0A) → [See the numbers](#numbers)

## What came back

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **41%** | no DMARC record286 of 700 |
| **14%** | DMARC at p=reject97 of 700 |
| **32%** | SPF soft-fail227 of 700 |
| **56** | fully enforcingSPF -all + p=reject |

| Check | Result | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Check | Result | Share |
| No DMARC record at all | 286 / 700 | 41% |
| DMARC p=none (detect, deliver anyway) | 156 | 22% |
| DMARC p=quarantine | 161 | 23% |
| DMARC p=reject (blocking) | 97 | 14% |
| No SPF record | 115 | 16% |
| SPF soft-fail (~all) | 227 | 32% |
| SPF hard-fail (-all) | 312 | 45% |
| No CAA record | 690 | 99% |

### Why p=none is not "we have DMARC"

p=none asks receiving servers to watch and report. It does not ask them to refuse anything. Spoofed mail claiming your domain is still delivered to the inbox — it is just marked, and users have been trained to click through that mark. p=reject is what turns "detect" into "do not deliver".

The path that works, and the order matters: start at p=quarantine with a rua= address, read the aggregate reports until the only senders listed are ones you recognise, then move to p=reject. Only after that tighten SPF from ~all to -all. Deploying -all before the reports are clean is the single most common way a DMARC rollout gets rolled back.

```console
_dmarc.yourdomain.org. IN TXT "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.org"
```

### The audit was wrong the first time, and that matters

An earlier pass resolved each RR set into one concatenated string and tested for a v=spf1 prefix, so any leading verification record broke the match and the domain came back as "no SPF". A second pass used a 3-second resolver timeout under 48-way concurrency and wrote those timeouts down as "record absent". Between them, 22 of the first 82 contact emails carried a finding that was not true.

All 22 were corrected by email the same day, and this page is generated from the corrected pass: parse per record, confirm with two or more resolvers, and if the answer is not confirmed, publish nothing rather than guess. A number in a report that gets forwarded to an auditor should survive dig.

| **Ingestion** | public procurement feeds |
| **KSC · NIS2** | risk scoring |
| **Export** | campaign-ready data |
| **Proprietary** | Hartwell Labs internal |

## What it does, concretely.

*Why scryer-core*

#### Ingestion

Continuous ingestion of public-procurement feeds — watch the tenders that matter, automatically.

#### Risk scoring

KSC/NIS2-informed scoring puts the highest-risk organizations at the top of the queue.

#### Campaign export

Campaign-ready output with per-lead mail briefs feeds our outreach tooling — no manual list wrangling.

#### Attack surface map

Passive DNS audit maps the external attack surface of every organization — context for outreach and for security reviews.

## Proprietary — access on request.

*Access*

scryer-core powers Hartwell Labs internal GTM and client engagements. We grant source access to partners under NDA — write to important@hartwell-labs.pl.

## CI on every push.

*Same discipline as everything we ship*

Tests, CodeQL static analysis and signed release assets with SBOM — enforced by the organization-wide engineering standards.

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.

## Page content

*Security*

# Found something? Tell us first.

We practice coordinated disclosure across all products. This page defines exactly what you can expect from us — response times, severity handling and legal safe harbor for researchers.

[Report a vulnerability](mailto:important@hartwell-labs.pl?subject=Security%20report%3A%20%5Bproduct%5D) → [security.txt](https://hartwell-labs.pl/.well-known/security.txt)

## How disclosure works

Send a report to the security contact below. Include a description, reproduction steps and affected product/version. We will:

48 hours
Acknowledgment.
You receive a confirmation with a tracking reference.
Days 2–7
Triage & severity.
We reproduce, classify per the table below and agree on a coordination timeline with you.
Fix
Remediation.
Patch developed, tested and released per the severity SLA. You get pre-release access to verify the fix.
Release
Public disclosure.
Advisory published with credit (opt-in). Nothing is published before a fix ships, unless the vulnerability is already being exploited.

### Severity & response targets

| Severity (CVSS 3.1) | Examples | Acknowledgment | Fix target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Severity (CVSS 3.1) | Examples | Acknowledgment | Fix target |
| Critical 9.0–10.0 | RCE, auth bypass, signature-verified pipeline escape | 48 hours | 7 days |
| High 7.0–8.9 | Privilege escalation, detection evasion by design | 48 hours | 30 days |
| Medium 4.0–6.9 | Info leaks, weak defaults in optional modes | 48 hours | 90 days |
| Low 0.1–3.9 | Hardening opportunities, documentation gaps | 48 hours | Best effort |

### Supported versions

| Product | Supported line | Latest release | Security fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product | Supported line | Latest release | Security fixes |
| talus-process-monitor | v0.8.x | v0.8.2 (2026-09-23) | Yes |
| Externum | v4.3.x | v4.3.0 (2026-09-23) | Yes |
| All other products | latest | see releases page | Yes |
| Older releases | — | — | Unsupported |

### Safe harbor

We consider security research conducted in good faith and in accordance with this policy to be authorized. We will not pursue legal action against researchers who: use only their own accounts and test data, avoid service degradation, give us reasonable time to remediate before public disclosure, and do not access data belonging to other users. If you are unsure whether your activity fits, contact us first — we will help you draw the line.

### Hall of Fame

No external reports yet — the list is empty on purpose, not by omission. If you find a real issue in our products, this is where your name goes.

Impatient? Try to break our products — the challenge lives in the hack-the-lab repository.

#### Your name here

opt-in credit

We credit only with your explicit consent — anonymous acknowledgment ("a friendly researcher") works just as well.

# Talus Field Guide — deployment & tuning playbook | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

On this page

← talus-process-monitor

## Talus Field Guide

Deployment & tuning playbook for real Linux servers. Written by the author — every flag here is a real interface of the agent, nothing invented.

### 1. Pick your deployment mode before anything else

| Mode | Command | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | Command | Use when |
| Observe | sudo process-monitor monitor | First week. Learn what normal looks like on YOUR hosts. Zero risk. |
| Pipeline | sudo process-monitor monitor --json | You already run a log stack (rsyslog, Loki, SIEM). Detection without response. |
| EDR | sudo process-monitor monitor --auto-kill | Hosts that hold things worth keeping, after tuning. Requires Enterprise license. |

Rule of thumb: never start in EDR mode. Tune in Observe, graduate to EDR. A wrong kill on a backup job is worse than a slow alert.

### 2. Install and sanity-check in five minutes

```
# Option A: pip installer (pulls the prebuilt release binary, no compiler needed) pip install talus-process-monitor talus-monitor install # downloads the agent from GitHub Releases # (v0.8.3: eBPF object is embedded — no .o install step) # Option B: cargo (builds from crates.io) cargo install process-monitor # Option C: build from source git clone https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/talus-process-monitor.git cd talus-process-monitor && ./build.sh # TUI variant, ~1.7MB # or: ./build.sh --web # + REST API, WebSocket, Prometheus (Enterprise) ./install.sh # user-local install (default) sudo ./install.sh --system # /usr/local system-wide # 5-second end-to-end self-diagnostic (eBPF loads? events flowing?): sudo process-monitor monitor --diagnose
```

If --diagnose completes cleanly, the pipeline works end-to-end on your kernel. If it fails: check you are root (or CAP_BPF/CAP_SYS_ADMIN, as in the Docker example), and that BTF is available (ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux).

### 3. Tuning the one knob that matters: the threshold

Talus alerts when a process opens N or more files within 1 second (default --alert-threshold 50). That single number is your false-positive dial:

    - Backups, sync jobs, media encoding — these legitimately touch hundreds of files per second. Run during a real backup window; if Talus flags the backup process, raise the threshold above the observed rate (e.g. --alert-threshold 400 ).
    - Typical web/API hosts — the default 50 rarely fires on legitimate traffic. Keep it.
    - Paranoid mode (tiny document sets, archives) — --alert-threshold 20 . Expect noise; tune or accept.

```
# Measure what normal looks like on this host: sudo process-monitor monitor --benchmark 30 # throughput + hot processes # Narrow the view to the file types you actually protect: sudo process-monitor monitor --filter-ext pdf sudo process-monitor monitor --filter-ext enc
```

FP triage method: run --json for 24h into a file, jq the alerts, and whitelist the two or three noisy legitimate processes by adjusting the threshold — not by disabling the agent. One evening of work, once per host type.

### 4. Ship it as a service

```
# /etc/systemd/system/talus.service [Unit] Description=Talus eBPF ransomware tripwire After=network.target [Service] ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/process-monitor monitor --json --alert-threshold 400 Restart=always RestartSec=5 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now talus journalctl -u talus -f # watch the NDJSON stream
```

### 5. MeMLP — the neural layer, when to switch it on

--memlp enables the online-training detection engine. It learns from live events and saves a checkpoint every 30 seconds:

```console
sudo process-monitor monitor --memlp --memlp-checkpoint /var/lib/talus/memlp.json
```

    - Switch it on after the threshold is sane — it learns from the stream you give it.
    - The checkpoint persists across restarts: the model you trained stays yours.

### 6. Enterprise wiring (license → dashboard → exports)

```
# Activate your license (no root required): process-monitor license activate KEY process-monitor license verify # Web dashboard + REST API + Prometheus (build with ./build.sh --web first): sudo process-monitor monitor --web 0.0.0.0:8080 --auto-kill # Stream detections into your data stack: sudo process-monitor monitor --auto-kill \ --kafka-brokers localhost:9092 --kafka-topic talus-detections \ --clickhouse http://localhost:8123 \ --memgraph http://localhost:7474
```

Kafka/ClickHouse/Memgraph flags are independent — wire only what your stack already has. Nothing leaves the host by default.

### 7. Runbook: an alert fired — now what

    - In Observe/Pipeline mode: identify the process from the JSON event (pid, comm, exe). If it is not a known job — stop it, snapshot the directory tree, check for rename chains and new .enc -style extensions.
    - In EDR mode: Talus already killed the process (SIGKILL at threshold breach). Verify with journalctl -u talus | grep kill , then preserve evidence before restoring from backup.
    - After any incident: re-run --diagnose , review whether the threshold should move, and keep the 24h JSON window as evidence.

### 8. Honest limits

    - Talus watches file-event behaviour . It is not an antivirus, not a network IDS, and it will not catch a threat that touches zero files.
    - eBPF requires BTF/CO-RE support (recent kernels; the Docker runbook mounts /sys/kernel/btf explicitly). Old LTS boxes need a plan.
    - One threshold for the whole host: workloads with wildly different IO profiles on one box need either separate hosts or a higher threshold.

### Frequently asked questions

Which Talus deployment mode should I start with?

Start in Observe mode (sudo process-monitor monitor) for about a week. It is detection-only with zero risk of a wrong kill, and it teaches you what normal file activity looks like on your hosts. Graduate to Pipeline mode (--json) when you run a log stack, and to EDR mode (--auto-kill) only after tuning, on hosts that hold things worth keeping.

How do I install Talus without a compiler?

pip install talus-process-monitor, then run talus-monitor install — the Python installer pulls the prebuilt release binary (~4 MB) from GitHub Releases, no Rust toolchain needed. Alternatively cargo install process-monitor builds from crates.io, or ./build.sh compiles from source.

What threshold should I set for Talus alerts?

Talus alerts when a process opens N or more files within 1 second (default --alert-threshold 50). Keep 50 on typical web/API hosts, raise it above the observed rate of legitimate write-heavy jobs like backups (e.g. --alert-threshold 400), or lower it to 20 in paranoid mode for tiny document sets. Run monitor --benchmark 30 to measure what normal looks like on your host first.

What Linux kernels does Talus support?

Talus needs eBPF with BTF/CO-RE support, which means recent kernels. Check with ls /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux — if that file exists, the agent loads. The Docker runbook mounts /sys/kernel/btf explicitly. Old LTS kernels without BTF need a separate plan; there is no kernel module fallback by design.

An alert fired — what do I do first?

Do not panic-kill. First identify the process from the alert output, then check whether it is a legitimate write-heavy job (backup, sync, media encoding) that simply crossed the threshold — if so, raise the threshold instead of disabling the agent. If the process is unknown, snapshot-preserve the target directories before any response, then pause or kill. The runbook section above walks through this decision step by step.

### Want the rest of the product?

Capabilities, the sixty-second start and the component licensing table are on the product page. The agent itself is free and MIT forever — the Enterprise license adds auto-kill, the web dashboard and the Kafka/ClickHouse exports.

## Page content

*Flagship · Rust · eBPF*

# Behavioral ransomware detection that answers with a kill signal.

talus-process-monitor hooks syscall tracepoints in the Linux kernel, scores per-process open-rates in one-second windows and terminates the encryptor with SIGKILL — guardrailed, whitelist-aware, and never at the cost of the host. One static binary. No kernel modules. No telemetry.

[Buy Enterprise — $50/node](https://buy.polar.sh/polar_cl_E577BTilme4dnUFsfbG0aE4qo7QILaugmEjsA0oajKK) → [Deployment guide](https://hartwell-labs.pl/docs#talus) → [Source ↗](https://github.com/Hartwell-Labs/talus-process-monitor)

| **7.6%** | sustained CPU under synthetic load |
| **<1s** | verdict to SIGKILL, same second |
| **188** | tests in the CI suite, every push |

## Three layers, one binary.

*What it does*

Detection is the easy half. Talus ships the half nobody writes up: the response path.

#### Detect: behavior, not signatures

Mass file-opens scored per process in 1s windows; canary reads, mass-delete and exfiltration-spike detectors. Signature-free — catches strains nobody has named yet.

#### Respond: SIGKILL in the same second

When the verdict fires, the offending process is killed immediately. Guardrails, per-path whitelists and canary verification keep it fast without being reckless.

#### Contain: Landlock & seccomp self-sandboxing

The agent sandboxes itself before it starts watching: no kernel modules, no writable footprint outside its own directory, verified by its own tests.

#### Ship: SIEM, Kafka, ClickHouse, MemGraph

Forward alerts as RFC5424 or CEF, stream raw events to Kafka, persist to ClickHouse, explore process lineage in MemGraph. Self-hosted, your infrastructure.

## From pip to live dashboard.

*Sixty-second start*

```console
pip install talus-process-monitor
```

```console
talus-monitor install
```

```console
sudo talus --web 10.0.0.5:8443
```

```console
talus-monitor selftest --canary
```

The canary self-test simulates a ransomware burst with harmless file operations and prints the real verdict — detection proof on your hardware in under a minute. Full flags and tuning: /docs and the Field Guide.

# TrustNode — a Solana-like validator written from scratch in Rust | Hartwell Labs

> Maszynowo czytelna wersja strony. Zawiera **pełną treść** oraz, niżej, **specyfikację wyglądu** — na wypadek, gdy AI nie może otworzyć strony.
> Konwencja plików dla AI: https://llmstxt.org — indeks `llms.txt`, wszystko `llms-full.txt`.

---

## Page content

*Trusted compute · Rust*

# Built to understand, not to fork.

A Solana-style validator written from scratch in Rust: proof-of-history clock, Tower BFT consensus, Sealevel-style parallel execution, Turbine propagation with real Reed–Solomon erasure coding, CRDS gossip over UDP, a fee-priority mempool and an SBF-inspired program executor. Not a wrapper. Not a fork. Every line mine.

[Source on GitHub ↩](https://github.com/BartoszOsiej/TrustNode) → [Documentation](https://wiki.hartwell-labs.pl/projects/solana-validator)

| Value | Label |
|---|---|
| **12** | crates in the Cargo workspace |
| **228** | tests, all public |
| **~1M** | PoH hashes per second |
| **MIT** | licensed, fully public |

## Eleven subsystems, all real.

*What is inside*

Every cryptographic path is implemented, not stubbed: transactions are Ed25519-verified, votes are signed before they touch state, gossip messages that fail verification are counted and dropped without a reply.

#### Proof of History

A verifiable delay function: N sequential SHA-256 hashes per tick. Verification re-hashes N times and checks the result matches.

#### Tower BFT

Fork choice with lockouts — every vote on the same fork doubles the lockout, so switching forks gets expensive. Finality at two-thirds supermajority.

#### Sealevel-style scheduler

Conflict analysis over read/write account sets. Disjoint transactions batch together; write conflicts serialise. Slot-based with a compute budget.

#### Turbine + Reed–Solomon

Systematic RS over GF(256): any k of n shards reconstruct the block exactly, or the decoder returns None. Shreds are signed and verified on receipt.

#### CRDS gossip

Cluster Replicated Data Store with versioning, timeouts, push/pull and ping/pong — every outgoing message signed.

#### Accounts DB

Append-only store with a DashMap index for O(1) lookups and a Merkle tree over state for a verifiable state root.

#### Fee-priority mempool

Transaction fees are charged against the real accounts DB even when an instruction later fails — because that is Solana semantics.

#### Program executor

A unified native dispatcher with a System program (real SOL transfers, account creation) and an SPL-like Token program. No SBF runtime, so an unsupported program fails honestly instead of faking an Ok.

#### JSON-RPC 2.0

Account queries over a real server, backed by the same state the consensus path commits to.

## Tests first, then the node.

*Run it*

228 tests across the workspace, cargo clippy -D warnings, cargo audit with zero advisories, and CI on Linux and macOS with --locked, plus CodeQL and the OpenSSF Scorecard.

```console
cargo test --workspace
```

```console
cargo bench -- --bench
```

## Research-grade, on purpose.

*What it is not*

No SBF runtime, no QUIC (the transport is real UDP), no snapshot loading, and nothing tuned for production throughput. It has never run on mainnet and we do not claim it has — the README says plainly: do not use it for real transactions or staking. What it demonstrates is that the architecture can be held in one head, end to end.

   - Zawartość: tekst (1 akapitów)
7. **Footer** — tło `--bg-subtle`, kolumny: Products, Resources, Company (8 linków), na dobie fine-print z licencją i krajem.

### 4. Interactive elements

- 2 przycisków **COPY** (`assets/site.js` → `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, tekst zmienia się na *COPIED* na 1400 ms). Każdy trzyma komendę w atrybucie `data-code`.
- 2 linków zewnętrznych (GitHub, PyPI, crates.io, sklepy) — otwierane w tej samej karcie.
- Brak formularzy, brak JS zależności poza `assets/site.js` i `challenge.js`.
- `challenge.js` jest skryptem łupieżczym — nie ładuj go przy renderowaniu.

### 5. Metadata for AI consumers

- `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<link rel="canonical">` — patrz frontmatter.
- Na stronie jest JSON-LD (`application/ld+json`) z typem `Organization` / `WebSite` / `SoftwareApplication`.
- Strona jest dostępna również jako ten plik `.md` oraz w `/llms-full.txt`.
